messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:


Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ramesh Patel is a 79-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment after years of carrying his war experience in near silence. He is divorced and still works shifts as a warehouse worker, a fact he describes with a kind of stubborn pride. He says work gives him “something to do with my hands,” though over time it has also become one more place where the past appears beside him without warning. When he first spoke about the trauma, he did not begin with abstract statements about war. He began with one scene: the noise, the confusion, and the certainty in that moment that he would die. In combat, he found himself surrounded by sudden blasts, shouted commands, and the sight of other men falling around him. What remained with him most was not a single neat memory but a series of sharply preserved fragments—the force of the sound, the air seeming to split, the feeling that nowhere was safe, and the terrible awareness that survival depended on reacting instantly while terrified.

In the weeks after he returned, Ramesh did what many people around him expected: he carried on. He worked, married, raised a family, and spoke very little about what had happened. Yet the war never settled into the past for him. He describes the memories as if they are stored in pieces, arriving suddenly and with more force than he thinks they should. A bang in everyday life can feel to him like more than a noise; for a moment it is as if his body has already decided where he is before his mind can catch up. He does not talk about these episodes dramatically. Instead he says, with frustration and embarrassment, that he “still reacts like it’s happening.” The sense of present danger has remained close to the surface for decades.

At the warehouse, this is especially hard. The setting is full of the kinds of moments that catch him off guard: pallets dropped too quickly, metal striking concrete, engines revving, voices raised across long aisles. Younger coworkers may laugh off the noise, but Ramesh feels his whole system tense. He scans automatically, noticing exits, movement, and anything out of place. He prefers tasks that let him keep some distance from others and some control over his surroundings. If a section of the warehouse is particularly loud or crowded, he finds reasons to stay away from it. He tells himself this is just common sense, but over the years it has narrowed his world. Coworkers know him as reliable but reserved. He joins no one for breaks if he can help it, and when people ask ordinary questions about his past, he redirects the conversation. The result has been a life that looks steady from the outside while becoming increasingly constricted.

His divorce sits in that same history of distance. He does not offer easy explanations, and he does not present himself as a victim of his symptoms. Still, as he talks, it is clear how much of himself he learned to hold back. He had come to believe that speaking about combat would bring something unbearable too close, and that if he let himself feel what was there, he would lose control. What frightened him most was not only remembering the war but the possibility of being overwhelmed by it in front of someone else. So he kept to routines, kept conversations shallow, and relied on work and endurance rather than closeness.

Now, at 79, he is struck by how little this private discipline has changed what he lives with inside. He reports severe PTSD symptoms overall, and what troubles him is how immediate the threat still feels despite the passage of time. Recently, after a loud crash at work, he found himself shaken enough that he had to stop what he was doing and steady himself against a shelf. He was deeply rattled by the thought that even now, in an ordinary warehouse in America, his body could respond as if he were back in combat. That incident, more than any abstract wish to “talk to someone,” brought him in. He says he is tired of organizing his life around what might set him off, tired of feeling as though danger is always one sound away. At the same time, he is wary of treatment. Part of him fears that revisiting the war will make it more vivid, not less. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is simple: to feel older than the war at last, and to get through a workday without bracing for battle.
